subject: Biology
title: The Discovery of Cells
description: A quick, practical guide to The Discovery of Cells.

hook.text: In 1665, Robert Hooke peered at cork through a microscope and saw tiny compartments.

buildup.text: He named them 'cells' after the small rooms monks lived in at monasteries.

discovery.text: Two centuries later, scientists proved every living thing is built from cells.

twist.text: A drop of pond water holds thousands of cells, each alive and working.

climax.text: Cell theory became biology's bedrock: all life is cells, all cells come from cells.

punchline.text: One slice of cork launched a whole science.

quiz.question: What did Robert Hooke see when he examined cork in 1665?

details.summary: Robert Hooke first observed cells in 1665 while examining cork under a microscope, naming them cells because they resembled monastery rooms. Anton van Leeuwenhoek later discovered living single-celled organisms, launching the era of microbiology and cell biology.
details.whyItMatters: The discovery of cells transformed our understanding of life from mystical to mechanical. It established that all living things share a common structural unit and opened the door to modern medicine, genetics, and biotechnology.
takeaways: Robert Hooke coined the term 'cell' in 1665 from cork observations
Van Leeuwenhoek first observed living microorganisms around 1674
The microscope was the enabling technology for the discovery of cells

faq.question: What did Robert Hooke actually see when he discovered cells?
faq.answer: Hooke saw the empty cell walls of dead plant cells in cork, which looked like small chambers or rooms. He was not seeing living cells or their contents. His observation revealed the structural building blocks of life even though the cells were long dead.

faq.question: Why was van Leeuwenhoek's contribution so important?
faq.answer: Van Leeuwenhoek was the first to observe living single-celled organisms, which he called animalcules. His handcrafted microscopes achieved 270x magnification, revealing bacteria, protists, and sperm cells that no human had ever seen before.
